content.title: About
content.content: Cheese, processed with vegetables is a ready‑to‑eat product made by blending grated cheese with various vegetable ingredients such as carrots, broccoli, or bell peppers. It is commonly used as a filling for sandwiches, casseroles, and quick meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of cheese and vegetables increases the vitamin and mineral content compared with plain cheese.
Vegetable additions can improve the flavor profile, making the product feel less fatty.
These products are often sold in single‑serve packages for convenient preparation.
In several countries they are a popular school snack.
The processing technology helps retain most of the vegetables' nutrients.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese is an excellent source of calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Processed cheese provides riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables add beta‑carotene, vitamin C and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The product supplies complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable content boosts dietary fiber, aiding normal digestion.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or lactose may experience reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed cheeses often contain added salt for flavor and preservation.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake can contribute to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain artificial preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese with vegetables is convenient in sandwiches, mixed into pasta, baked in the oven, used as a filling for omelets, or simply as a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors, color changes, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: A waffle is a light, crisp pastry made from a batter of flour, eggs, milk, and butter. It is often served with fruit, berries, cream, or syrup and is a popular fast‑food item in restaurants and cafés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles originated in medieval Europe and were originally cooked in specialized iron plates.
There are many batter variations: classic, Belgian, yeast‑leavened, and gluten‑free.
Waffles are frequently used as a base for desserts—waffle cakes, ice cream in waffle cones, etc.
Both sweet and savory versions exist, with cheese, ham, or vegetables added to the batter.
Waffles store well because their low moisture content keeps them crunchy.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in the batter provide quick energy, making waffles a good breakfast option.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter supplies thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk add a modest amount of animal protein.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: Dairy contributes calcium, while whole‑grain flour adds iron.

items.title: Pairs well with fruit
items.content: Adding berries or sliced fruit boosts fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet waffles can contain a lot of sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics or weight‑control diets.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional waffles are made with wheat flour, posing a problem for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Butter in the batter raises calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Processed additives
items.content: Pre‑made mixes may contain preservatives and artificial flavors.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve waffles hot with honey, maple syrup, berry sauce, fresh fruit, or whipped cream. Restaurants often top them with ham, cheese, and vegetables for a savory version. For a healthier choice, use whole‑grain flour and limit added sugar and butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked waffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in a toaster or oven to restore crispness.
